summary: This memo updates RFC 3168, which defines Explicit Congestion Notification. It relaxes restrictions that hindered experiments aiming at benefits beyond avoiding packet loss, and summarizes the areas where experimentation is expected.

eli5.summary: The old rules stopped people from trying new ideas for how to handle traffic jams. This loosens them so researchers can test.

subtitle: A process memo that loosens old ECN rules so researchers can run congestion experiments, provided each is approved in an Experimental RFC.

tldr.problem: RFC 3168, a Proposed Standard, forbids several uses of ECN that experimenters want to try, so each experiment would need a standards process exception.
tldr.mechanism: This memo updates RFC 3168 and related RTP and DCCP RFCs with an escape clause, "unless otherwise specified by an Experimental RFC in the IETF document stream". It also retires the ECN nonce experiment.
tldr.outcome: Three areas of experimentation are now allowed without further exceptions, each requiring its own Experimental RFC that discusses congestion control implications. RFC 3540 is reclassified as Historic.

today: RFC 8311 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3168, RFC 4341, RFC 4342, RFC 5622 and RFC 6679, and records that RFC 3540 is Historic.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3168 specifies Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), a way for the network to tell endpoints about congestion without dropping packets. RFC 3168 is a Proposed Standard, so any experiment that contradicts it would need a standards process exception. This memo avoids that by updating RFC 3168 once, for all experiments in three named areas.

An Experimental RFC in the IETF document stream is still required to take advantage of the updates. The memo expresses no view on the likely outcome of the experiments and does not specify them in detail. Standards Track RFCs do not need these updates, because any of them can update RFC 3168 directly.

Related updates are made to the ECN specification for RTP (RFC 6679) and for three DCCP profiles (RFC 4341, RFC 4342 and RFC 5622).
sections.eli5: Some rules were too strict for people who wanted to test new ideas. This memo opens a door for testing, as long as each test is written down and approved first.

sections.title: Three Areas of Experimentation
sections.content:
The IP header's ECN field has codepoints: Not-ECT (sender is not ECN capable), ECT(0) and ECT(1) (both mean ECN capable) and CE (Congestion Experienced, set by a network node as congestion rises). The memo covers three areas.

  • Congestion Response Differences: a CE mark suggests a short queue at the bottleneck, so a sender might back off by a smaller amount than it would after a loss.
  • Congestion Marking Differences: network nodes might treat ECT(1) traffic differently from ECT(0), for example to keep very shallow queues, paired with a different sender response.
  • TCP Control Packets and Retransmissions: ECN might be extended to packets such as SYNs and to retransmissions.

Any Experimental RFC that uses these updates must discuss the congestion control implications, so that deployment does not pose a congestion-based threat to the Internet.
sections.eli5: People want to try three new things: reacting more gently to a warning, giving some traffic a faster lane, and using warnings on more kinds of packets.

sections.title: Retiring the ECN Nonce
sections.content:
RFC 3168 assigned the ECT(1) codepoint to the ECN nonce, an anti-cheating feature specified in RFC 3540 that discourages receivers from exploiting ECN to gain throughput at others' expense. The nonce works as specified and was deployed in limited environments, but widespread use never materialized.

A study using 2014 data on the top one million web servers found that, after ECN was negotiated, none of the 581,711 IPv4 servers tested used both ECT codepoints. Of the 17,028 IPv6 servers tested, four set both, which might have been nonce use or might have been erroneous re-marking by a middlebox or router.

Since new experiments need ECT(1), reserving it for the nonce is no longer justified. This memo declares the nonce experiment concluded, reclassifies RFC 3540 from Experimental to Historic, and removes nonce discussion from RFC 3168 in four places. IANA also marks bit 7 of the TCP header flags (formerly NS, Nonce Sum) as Reserved.
sections.eli5: One of the two special markers was saved for a cheat-catching trick that almost nobody used. Since it sat unused, it is being freed up for new experiments.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 3168
sections.content:
Each change inserts the words "unless otherwise specified by an Experimental RFC in the IETF document stream" into a rule.

  • Response to CE: RFC 3168 required the response to a CE-marked packet to be essentially the same as to a single dropped packet, and said TCP should halve cwnd and reduce ssthresh on an ECN-Echo. Both may now differ.
  • Router treatment: routers may treat ECT(0) and ECT(1) differently, and CE marks may be applied where the router would not otherwise have dropped the packet.
  • Which codepoint: protocols and senders MUST use ECT(0) and MUST NOT use ECT(1) unless an Experimental RFC says otherwise.
  • TCP control packets: ECT may be used on SYN and SYN-ACK packets, pure acknowledgements, window probes and retransmissions.

Marking experiments SHOULD change network behavior for ECT(1) rather than ECT(0) if only one is changed, and MUST NOT change ECT(0) behavior in a way that needs sender changes. If ECT(1) marking changes require a new sender response, the Experimental RFC MUST specify that response and any router forwarding changes for CE-marked packets.

Middleboxes SHOULD NOT discard TCP control packets and retransmissions solely because the ECN field is not Not-ECT. The exception is responding to an attack, and such discarding MUST NOT be routine.
sections.eli5: The old rule book said always, never and the same for everyone. Now each rule has an added line: unless an approved experiment says differently.

sections.title: RTP, DCCP and Network Guidance
sections.content:
For RTP, RFC 6679 is updated so that random ECT values MUST NOT be used and ECT(0) MUST be used unless an Experimental RFC says otherwise. Its rule that the reaction to CE must be the same as to loss is also made conditional on the same escape clause.

For DCCP, the three profiles said data packets are sent with either ECT(0) or ECT(1). They now say such senders MUST set ECT(0) unless an Experimental RFC specifies otherwise, and nonce discussion is removed.

The memo also gives guidance to everyone else. Routers not in an experiment should keep treating ECT(0) and ECT(1) as equivalent. Network nodes SHOULD NOT assume a CE mark means the packet would have been dropped, and a node MUST NOT originate ECT(1) traffic unless it takes part in a Congestion Marking Differences experiment. Anything that monitors traffic should expect ECN on packets that do not use it today. Experimenters should consider operations and management impacts.
sections.eli5: Other protocols get the same permission slip, and everybody else is asked to keep behaving as before unless they are in an approved experiment.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As a process memo that only relaxes restrictions on experimentation, it says there are no protocol security considerations. Security considerations for each experiment belong in the documents that propose it.

The memo does stress that effective congestion control is crucial to the Internet. It places the responsibility for not breaking it on the experiments and their authors. Review by the IETF community and the IESG before publication is intended to give assurance that each experiment does not break Internet congestion control.
sections.eli5: The memo is only permission to test, so the safety checking is the job of whoever proposes each test.
